newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary rejects farmers' threat to block borders.
newsitem.headline: Hungary rejects farmers' threat to block borders.

text.p: Hungary's ruling Socialist Party on Tuesday rejected a farmers' union ultimatum to block border crossings within 72 hours unless their tax relief demands are met.
"The government cannot tolerate such actions," Gabor Kiss, Socialist Party presidium member, told Reuters.

Representatives of farmers' union METESZ sent an ultimatum to the government on Monday saying they would block border crossings and roads leading into the capital unless their demand for unconditional tax relief for farmers earning less than 1.5 million forints ($8,500) a year is met.
"One real measure of a union is how prepared it is for meaningful talks," Kiss said.
Kiss spoke after a meeting with another farmers' union, MAGOSZ, whose representatives put forward a 12-point list of demands for a comprehensive overhaul of Hungary's ailing agriculture sector.
"We did not give the government a deadline, but would like to see our demands met within a reasonable time," MAGOSZ President Huba Kozma said.
He added that for the time being they do not support METESZ's ultimatum.
A February demonstration in the central Hungarian town of Kiskoros sparked a series of farmer protests following 1997 income and social security tax increases for individual farmers.
The government made a set of initial concessions to the farmers who have since formed METESZ. The ultimatum is to be submitted for emergency parliamentary debate this week.

METESZ has since asked for further concessions and analysts said the move could trigger a chain reaction as larger farmers' unions also have to resort to action in order to hold on to their increasingly dissatisfied members.
Government officials have repeatedly said Hungary's agriculture sector, which has seen output plummet 40 percent since the mid 1980s, is in urgent need of an overhaul.

Agriculture Minister Frigyes Nagy last week announced a nationwide debate on the ministry's recently devised 10-year farming policy draft, hoping to defuse the situation, but farmers said the plan did not go beyond largely meaningless generalities.
